before.problem:
The migration table below describes the movement of the population between cities and suburbs every year in a certain state. 

|  |  | From: |  |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
|  |  | **Cities** | **Suburbs** |
| To: | **Cities** | $0.8$ | $0.7$ |
| **Suburbs** | $0.2$ | $0.3$ |  |

That is, $20%$ of those living in cities move to the suburbs each year, and $70%$ of those living in suburbs move to the cities.

Assuming that the population of the state is $9$ million and remains constant, how many people would eventually live in cities if the given probabilities remain constant over many years?

Question 1
?

The migration table below describes the movement of the population between cities and suburbs every year in a certain state.

From:
Cities Suburbs
To: Cities 0.8 0.7
Suburbs 0.2 0.3

That is, 20% of those living in cities move to the suburbs each year, and 70% of those living in suburbs move to the cities.

Assuming that the population of the state is 9 million and remains constant, how many people would eventually live in cities if the given probabilities remain constant over many years?

a
9 million
b
7 million
c
8.5 million
d
3 million
e
6.5 million
Submit

decision.explanation: At steady state, migration balances: 0.2C = 0.7S. With C + S = 9 million, 0.2C = 0.7(9 − C), so 0.9C = 6.3 and C = 7 million.

after.name: Question 1
after.problem:
The migration table below describes the movement of the population between cities and suburbs every year in a certain state. 

|  |  | From: |  |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
|  |  | **Cities** | **Suburbs** |
| To: | **Cities** | $0.8$ | $0.7$ |
| **Suburbs** | $0.2$ | $0.3$ |  |

That is, $20%$ of those living in cities move to the suburbs each year, and $70%$ of those living in suburbs move to the cities.

Assuming that the population of the state is $9$ million and remains constant, how many people would eventually live in cities if the given probabilities remain constant over many years?
after.worked_solution:
From the table, we get the corresponding stochastic matrix 

$$
P=[\begin{aligned}0.8 & 0.7 \\ 0.2 & 0.3\end{aligned}].
$$

Notice that $P$ contains only positive entries. So, the matrix $P$ is regular. As a result, after many years, the distribution will eventually converge to the unique steady-state vector of $P,$ and this convergence does not depend on the initial state.

Recall that a steady-state vector of a stochastic matrix $P$ is a stochastic vector $q$ such that 

$$
\begin{aligned}Pq=q\,⟹\,(P-I)q=0.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing $P-I,$ we get

$$
P-I=[\begin{aligned}0.8 & 0.7 \\ 0.2 & 0.3\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-0.2 & 0.7 \\ 0.2 & -0.7\end{aligned}].
$$

So, the matrix equation $(P-I)q=0$ is equivalent to the system of linear equations with the augmented matrix $M,$ which we reduce to row echelon form using Gaussian elimination as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}-0.2 & 0.7 & 0 \\ 0.2 & -0.7 & 0\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}-0.2 & 0.7 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix above has one pivot column (the $1$st one). Thus, ${x}_{2}$ is a free variable. From the first equation, we obtain 

$$
{x}_{1}=\frac{7}{2}{x}_{2}.
$$

Hence, the general solution is

$$
[\begin{aligned}\frac{7}{2}{x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{2}\in R.
$$

Since the steady-state vector must be stochastic, its entries should add up to $1.$ Therefore, we have 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{7}{2}{x}_{2}+{x}_{2} & =1 \\ \frac{9}{2}{x}_{2} & =1 \\ {x}_{2} & =\frac{2}{9}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
q=[\begin{aligned}\frac{7}{9} \\ \frac{2}{9}\end{aligned}].
$$

So, after many years, $\frac{7}{9}$ of the $9$ million population will live in cities. Therefore, the total number of people living in cities after many years will be

$$
\frac{7}{9}\cdot 9\,\text{million}=7\,\text{million}.
$$

after.name: Question 2
after.problem:
$$
P=[\begin{aligned}0 & 0.6 \\ 1 & 0.4\end{aligned}],\,q=[\begin{aligned}a \\ b\end{aligned}]
$$

Given that $q$ is the steady-state vector of the stochastic matrix $P,$ what is the value of $a-b?$
after.worked_solution:
Recall that a steady-state vector of a stochastic matrix $P$ is a stochastic vector $q$ such that 

$$
\begin{aligned}Pq & =q \\ Pq-q & =0 \\ Pq-Iq & =0 \\ (P-I)q & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing $P-I,$ we get

$$
P-I=[\begin{aligned}0 & 0.6 \\ 1 & 0.4\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-1 & 0.6 \\ 1 & -0.6\end{aligned}].
$$

The matrix equation $(P-I)q=0$ is equivalent to the system of linear equations with the augmented matrix $M,$ which we reduce to row echelon form using Gaussian elimination as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}-1 & 0.6 & 0 \\ 1 & -0.6 & 0\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}-1 & 0.6 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix above has one pivot column (the $1$st one). Thus, ${x}_{2}$ is a free variable. From the first equation, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}-{x}_{1}+0.6{x}_{2} & =0 \\ -{x}_{1}+\frac{3}{5}{x}_{2} & =0 \\ {x}_{1} & =\frac{3}{5}{x}_{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, the general solution is

$$
[\begin{aligned}\frac{3}{5}{x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{2}\in R.
$$

Since the steady-state vector must be stochastic, its entries should add up to $1.$ Therefore, we have 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{3}{5}{x}_{2}+{x}_{2} & =1 \\ \frac{8}{5}{x}_{2} & =1 \\ {x}_{2} & =\frac{5}{8}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
q=[\begin{aligned}a \\ b\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}\frac{3}{8} \\ \frac{5}{8}\end{aligned}].
$$

Finally, $a-b=\frac{3}{8}-\frac{5}{8}=-\frac{1}{4}.$

Recall that a steady-state vector of a stochastic matrix P is a stochastic vector q such that

Pq=qPq−q=0Pq−Iq=0(P−I)q=0.

Computing P−I, we get

P−I=[00.610.4]−[1001]=[−10.61−0.6].

The matrix equation (P−I)q=0 is equivalent to the system of linear equations with the augmented matrix M, which we reduce to row echelon form using Gaussian elimination as follows:

M=[−10.601−0.60]R2:=R2+R1∼[−10.60000]

The reduced matrix above has one pivot column (the 1st one). Thus, x2 is a free variable. From the first equation, we obtain −x1+0.6x2=0−x1+35x2=0x1=35x2

Hence, the general solution is [35x2x2],x2∈R.

Since the steady-state vector must be stochastic, its entries should add up to 1. Therefore, we have

content.problem:
$$
P=[\begin{aligned}0 & 0.6 \\ 1 & 0.4\end{aligned}],\,q=[\begin{aligned}a \\ b\end{aligned}]
$$

Given that $q$ is the steady-state vector of the stochastic matrix $P,$ what is the value of $a-b?$
content.worked_solution:
Recall that a steady-state vector of a stochastic matrix $P$ is a stochastic vector $q$ such that 

$$
\begin{aligned}Pq & =q \\ Pq-q & =0 \\ Pq-Iq & =0 \\ (P-I)q & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing $P-I,$ we get

$$
P-I=[\begin{aligned}0 & 0.6 \\ 1 & 0.4\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-1 & 0.6 \\ 1 & -0.6\end{aligned}].
$$

The matrix equation $(P-I)q=0$ is equivalent to the system of linear equations with the augmented matrix $M,$ which we reduce to row echelon form using Gaussian elimination as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}-1 & 0.6 & 0 \\ 1 & -0.6 & 0\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}-1 & 0.6 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix above has one pivot column (the $1$st one). Thus, ${x}_{2}$ is a free variable. From the first equation, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}-{x}_{1}+0.6{x}_{2} & =0 \\ -{x}_{1}+\frac{3}{5}{x}_{2} & =0 \\ {x}_{1} & =\frac{3}{5}{x}_{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, the general solution is

$$
[\begin{aligned}\frac{3}{5}{x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{2}\in R.
$$

Since the steady-state vector must be stochastic, its entries should add up to $1.$ Therefore, we have 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{3}{5}{x}_{2}+{x}_{2} & =1 \\ \frac{8}{5}{x}_{2} & =1 \\ {x}_{2} & =\frac{5}{8}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
q=[\begin{aligned}a \\ b\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}\frac{3}{8} \\ \frac{5}{8}\end{aligned}].
$$

Finally, $a-b=\frac{3}{8}-\frac{5}{8}=-\frac{1}{4}.$

decision.explanation: Since Pq = q and a + b + c = 1, the third row gives c = 0.2(a + b) + 0.4c = 0.2(1 − c) + 0.4c. Thus 0.8c = 0.2, so c = 1/4. Therefore a + b − c = 1 − 2c = 1/2.

after.name: Question 3
after.problem:
$$
P=[\begin{aligned}0.4 & 0.4 & 0.4 \\ 0.4 & 0.4 & 0.2 \\ 0.2 & 0.2 & 0.4\end{aligned}],\,q=[\begin{aligned}a \\ b \\ c\end{aligned}]
$$

Given that $q$ is the steady-state vector of the stochastic matrix $P$ shown above, what is the value of $a+b-c?$
after.worked_solution:
Recall that a steady-state vector of a stochastic matrix $P$ is a stochastic vector $q$ such that 

$$
\begin{aligned}Pq & =q \\ Pq-q & =0 \\ Pq-Iq & =0 \\ (P-I)q & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing $P-I,$ we get

$$
P-I=[\begin{aligned}0.4 & 0.4 & 0.4 \\ 0.4 & 0.4 & 0.2 \\ 0.2 & 0.2 & 0.4\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-0.6 & 0.4 & 0.4 \\ 0.4 & -0.6 & 0.2 \\ 0.2 & 0.2 & -0.6\end{aligned}].
$$

The matrix equation $(P-I)q=0$ is equivalent to the system of linear equations with the augmented matrix $M,$ which we reduce to row echelon form using Gaussian elimination as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}-0.6 & 0.4 & 0.4 & 0 \\ 0.4 & -0.6 & 0.2 & 0 \\ 0.2 & 0.2 & -0.6 & 0\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{1}:=10{R}_{1} \\ {R}_{2}:=10{R}_{2} \\ {R}_{3}:=10{R}_{3}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}-6 & 4 & 4 & 0 \\ 4 & -6 & 2 & 0 \\ 2 & 2 & -6 & 0\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{3}↔{R}_{1}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}2 & 2 & -6 & 0 \\ 4 & -6 & 2 & 0 \\ -6 & 4 & 4 & 0\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{2}:={R}_{2}-2{R}_{1} \\ {R}_{3}:={R}_{3}+3{R}_{1}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}2 & 2 & -6 & 0 \\ 0 & -10 & 14 & 0 \\ 0 & 10 & -14 & 0\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{3}:={R}_{3}+{R}_{2}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}2 & 2 & -6 & 0 \\ 0 & -10 & 14 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix above has two pivot columns (the $1$st and $2$nd). Thus, ${x}_{3}$ is a free variable. From the second equation, we obtain 

$$
{x}_{2}=\frac{14}{10}{x}_{3}=\frac{7}{5}{x}_{3}.
$$

 
Substituting this into the first equation, we obtain

$$
2{x}_{1}+2(\frac{7}{5}{x}_{3})-6{x}_{3}=0\,⟹\,{x}_{1}=\frac{8}{5}{x}_{3}.
$$

Hence, the general solution is

$$
[\begin{aligned}\frac{8}{5}{x}_{3} \\ \frac{7}{5}{x}_{3} \\ {x}_{3}\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{3}\in R.
$$

Since the steady-state vector must be stochastic, its entries should add up to $1.$ Therefore, we have 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{8}{5}{x}_{3}+\frac{7}{5}{x}_{3}+{x}_{3} & =1 \\ \frac{20}{5}{x}_{3} & =1 \\ {x}_{3} & =\frac{1}{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
q=[\begin{aligned}a \\ b \\ c\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}\frac{2}{5} \\ \frac{7}{20} \\ \frac{1}{4}\end{aligned}].
$$

Finally, 

$$
a+b-c=\frac{2}{5}+\frac{7}{20}-\frac{1}{4}=\frac{10}{20}=\frac{1}{2}.
$$

Question 3

P=[0.40.40.40.40.40.20.20.20.4],q=[abc]

Given that q is the steady-state vector of the stochastic matrix P shown above, what is the value of a+b−c?

a
12
b
14
c
13
d

25

Incorrect
EXPLANATION

Recall that a steady-state vector of a stochastic matrix P is a stochastic vector q such that

Pq=qPq−q=0Pq−Iq=0(P−I)q=0.

Computing P−I, we get

P−I=[0.40.40.40.40.40.20.20.20.4]−[100010001]=[−0.60.40.40.4−0.60.20.20.2−0.6].

The matrix equation (P−I)q=0 is equivalent to the system of linear equations with the augmented matrix M, which we reduce to row echelon form using Gaussian elimination as follows:

M=[−0.60.40.400.4−0.60.200.20.2−0.60]R1:=10R1R2:=10R2R3:=10R3∼[−64404−62022−60]R3↔R1∼[22−604−620−6440]R2:=R2−2R1R3:=R3+3R1∼[22−600−10140010−140]R3:=R3+R2∼[22−600−101400000]

The reduced matrix above has two pivot columns (the 1st and 2nd). Thus, x3 is a free variable. From the second equation, we obtain x2=1410x3=75x3. Substituting this into the first equation, we obtain 2x1+2(75x3)−6x3=0⟹x1=85x3. Hence, the general solution is [85x375x3x3],x3∈R.

Since the steady-state vector must be stochastic, its entries should add up to 1. Therefore, we have 85x3+75x3+x3=1205x3=1x3=14.

Therefore, q=[abc]=[2572014].

Finally, a+b−c=25+720−14=1020=12.
